summary:
Ekiti State stands under Nigeria's national framework, but Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe' documents enforcement and violence specific to the state. On 21 January 2014, days after the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened her with '14 years in prison'. The report states she was beaten at least twice over the period.

Debbie was unable to use Ekiti's health services safely and travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, indicating that routine care within the state carried an unacceptable risk of exposure.

Police and state officials in Ekiti used detention and extortion against gay men during 2014. In September 2014, a gay man was arrested at the Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti, his third arrest, and released after two days in detention after paying 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend. Separately in 2014, a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti.
tangentialFactors:
The pattern in Ekiti mirrors documented national enforcement elsewhere in Nigeria, where police have carried out mass arrests at social venues and where LGBTQ Nigerians report that the SSMPA has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination beyond its stated scope. Ekiti's documented incidents are individual rather than mass-arrest cases, but they show the same combination of physical violence, police detention and money demands.

The chilling of health-care access seen in Ekiti, where Debbie had to leave the state for HIV treatment, aligns with national reporting that many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and that activists say the Act hampers access to HIV prevention services.
localsOnly:
Ekiti State residents live under the national SSMPA regime, and Human Rights Watch records that within the state the law has been invoked alongside extralegal violence: a transgender woman was beaten by a group in Ado Ekiti who cited the Act's 14-year penalty, and gay men were arrested, detained and made to pay for release. A state investigator was also recorded extorting a young gay man in Ado Ekiti in 2014.

Health services within Ekiti were not usable safely for at least one trans resident, who travelled to Ibadan for HIV treatment rather than seek care locally.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Rights Watch material on Ekiti dates from 2014, with the report published in October 2016; no more recent Ekiti-specific enforcement or incident data appears in the source inventory, so the current on-the-ground picture in the state is unresolved.

Whether Ekiti State has any specific sub-national policy, police directive or protection mechanism for trans and gender-nonconforming residents is not sourced here.
